article_title: Your Ultimate Rakhi Style Guide For A Festive Ready Look | Femina.in
sub_title: Discover stunning Rakhi outfit ideas, from elegant sarees and shararas to contemporary cape sets and lehengas for a stylish festive look.
article_content: If sarees are your forever festive favourite, this blush pink number from Saika’s Echoes of Home: Pink City collection deserves a spot on your Rakhi moodboard. The lightweight, fluid drape is finished with a fine gota patti border, while the structured sleeveless blouse features metallic chevron embroidery for just the right amount of shimmer. It’s feminine, graceful and quietly striking. Pair it with a layered pearl choker and matching chandelier earrings. A low textured bun and soft pink makeup will complete the romantic look beautifully. If you love an outfit that feels effortlessly chic, the Dinah Short Jacket by Payal Jain is a beautiful place to start. Crafted in ivory cotton, it features refined cutwork and delicate lace overlays that add a breezy, feminine touch. Its open front and tailored yet airy silhouette make it perfect for layering without feeling too dressed up. If you love the bohemian-luxe aesthetic, layer it over a tonal embroidered maxi dress or skirt. For a more contemporary look, pair it with high-waisted trousers, a structured bustier and statement earrings. For those who believe festive dressing should make an entrance, the Mastani Lehenga Set from Riddhi Mehra’s Saaz collection brings all the drama. The strapless corset is richly embellished with antique gold zardozi and finished with hanging fringe droplets at the waist, while the sweeping floral lehenga adds movement and grandeur. Don’t shy away from the glamour. A jewelled choker, soft smoky eyes, luminous skin and sleek swept-back hair will make this look feel celebration-ready. Prefer something modern but still festive? This beige asymmetrical cape set from Vvani by Vats’ Jhoomar collection could be the one. The flowing georgette cape tunic is paired with tailored slim-fit trousers, while linear cascades of pearl and bead embroidery add movement to the scalloped hem and detailed cuffs. Let the silhouette do the talking with a pearl choker, metallic strappy heels and an architectural clutch. Keep your hair pulled back into a sleek low bun to highlight the cape’s elegant shape. If understated elegance is more your style, take a look at the Champagne Bloom Kurta Set from Ranna Gill’s Aura collection. The muted metallic palette of champagne, antique gold and deep bronze feels luxe without being overwhelming. Intricate hand embroidery traces the scalloped V-neckline and sheer sleeves, creating dimensional floral motifs against a luminous organza base. Keep the warm metallic tones in focus with emerald drop earrings, gold juttis and sleek, open hair. It’s an especially lovely choice for a daytime Rakhi celebration when you want to look polished without going overboard.

Limited Edt’s Superstar Consortium – Made in India features peacock motifs, textile-inspired vines, and details inspired by festive embroidery and old havelis. Only 350 numbered pairs are up for grabs, making this one a pretty special addition to any sneaker rotation. The GL002 Sprinter brings a little ’60s track nostalgia to your everyday sneaker rotation. The Tezz Green pairs its low-profile shape with rich textures, breathable materials, and handcrafted details. It’s got that vintage runner energy, but with a polished enough finish to work with your everyday outfits.

article_title: Inside Moonlit Palace: Anamika Khanna's Ode to Light, Legacy and The Women Who Preserve Craft | Femina.in
sub_title: Anamika Khanna opens India Couture Week 2026 with her collection ‘Moonlit Palace’ - a couture ode to craft, light and women's artistry.
article_content: Anamika Khanna unveiled her latest couture collection, ‘Moonlit Palace’, in a runway presentation at Taj Falaknuma Palace in Hyderabad as the inaugural show of Hyundai India Couture Week 2026, in association with Nexxus New York, an FDCI initiative that brought the house's craft-led philosophy to life through light, movement and atmosphere. The show opened in a space bathed in soft, silvered lighting, evoking the interior of a palace at night. The effect was immediate — understated, luminous and quietly dramatic — setting the tone for a collection built on contrast and craftsmanship. The opening looks moved with a deliberate, unhurried grace. Each drape fell in soft, considered folds, echoing themes of ritual and inheritance that run through the collection. Jewellery was integrated directly into the garments rather than layered on top, appearing as part of each piece's construction rather than a finishing touch. The second movement was inspired by Barmer, a town not far from where Anamika was born. This movement celebrated the town's rich textile traditions and was marked by a noticeable shift in colour and energy. It featured rich, saturated tones and intricate mirrorwork caught the light with every step, while gold foil detailing added moments of brilliance across the fabric. These textiles, developed in collaboration with women's craft communities in Barmer, were reworked through dyeing, embroidery and hand-painting, allowing traditional techniques to take on new life within a couture context. The third movement, Kalighat, drew inspiration from evenings spent with Kolkata's riverside art community. Silhouettes softened, with more fluid lines and refined proportions reflecting the grace and stillness associated with this artistic tradition. The pace of the show slowed here, allowing each garment's detailing and movement to take centre stage. With every passing movement, light played a more crucial role in highlighting the interplay between texture and shadow, with embroidery and metallic threadwork catching and releasing light as models moved. This visual rhythm reinforced the collection's central idea: craftsmanship as something dynamic, not static. The show closed with a final sequence that brought traditional and contemporary design influences together, mirroring the collection's introduction and creating a cohesive, full-circle presentation. The idea that held every diverse movement together was the exploration of clothing as a keeper of stories, carrying traces of hands, histories and identities across time. Moonlit Palace imagines a lost civilisation not as something forgotten, but as something continually rediscovered through craft and adornment, with every silhouette emerging as an archetype, shaped by an intimate dialogue between the body and ornament, tradition and reinvention. At its heart, this evening was a celebration of the women whose labour, intuition and artistry have preserved cultural narratives across generations. Anamika Khanna: Pushing Boundaries

article_title: 8 Styling Hacks to Elevate a Simple Midi Dress With Statement Accessories | Femina.in
sub_title: Discover how gold jewellery, belts, hats, bags, shoes & more add colours and personality to your midi dresses.
article_content: When we picture the perfect summer vacation, we imagine a flowy midi dress dancing in the sea breeze, a messy bun, a straw hat, comfy slip-ons, and the joy of watching the sunrise by the beach. Somehow, a midi dress just belongs in every summer memory. It's the one piece you can throw on without thinking, and with a few fun accessories, it can look completely different every single time. If you're looking to get more out of your favourite midi dress, these 8 styling hacks are all you need. 1. Layer On Gold Jewellery Image: Instagram Every plain, warm coloured midi dress deserves a touch of golden shine. Stack delicate chains, hoops, bangles, watches, and chunky rings to elevate your look. Wear delicate ones if you prefer minimalism, or layer accessories to make it look intentionally shiny. This instantly shifts your midi dress from basic to sleek luxury. 2. Cinch It With A Statement Belt Image: Instagram A Stylish belt elevates your midi dress and flares your curves. Pair a wide leather belt for a professional look, a metallic one for evening glamour, or a woven belt for relaxed beachwear. A corset belt, midi dress and boots are a powerful combo that never goes out of style. Image: Instagram A bag is an add-on to most fits; pair it with a midi dress, and it steals the spotlight. Think of beaded handbags, woven totes, colourful shoulder bags, or sparkly clutches. Any simple dress instantly looks styled when the bag brings the texture, colour, or shine.Preferably carry tote bags to achieve an enhanced, casual look. 5. Add Indian Jewellery Accents 6.Tie On A Bandana Image: Instagram Want a cool and soft look at the same time? Tie a bandana or scarf around your hair; it pops the colour and personality of the look. Pair it with a plain-coloured or minimal midi dress to let the bandana be the statement piece. Low effort, high impact. 7. Swap Basic Footwear For Statement Shoes Image: Instagram When the midi dress is flowy and fluid, add chunky sneakers, tie-up flats, or knee-high boots to elevate the outfit. With a midi dress, footwear is everything. It’s visible, intentional, and it sets the tone for the whole look. 8. Finish With Oversized Sunglasses Image: Instagram The summer calls for this powerful duo: midi dress and oversized sunglasses. Try pairing a contrasting shade with your outfit for a stylish and trendy look. Even if you don’t wear them on your eyes, sunglasses work as an accessory. article_content: At FDCI India Couture Week, Falguni Shane Peacock unveiled Le Grand Voyage — a collection inspired by the timeless romance of travel and the beauty of cultural exchange. The collection translated these influences into intricately hand-embroidered lehengas, sculpted corsets, dramatic capes, embellished tapestry jackets and exquisitely crafted sherwanis. article_title: Is The Bandana Scarf Making a Comeback This Summer? 7 Chic Ways to Style It | Femina.in
sub_title: Bandana scarfs are making a comeback this summer season, with own vintage flair and contemporary touch. Explore the various styles to wear these scarfs for your day.
article_content: One accessory that could definitely be listed among those that you will be able to spot this season is the bandana scarf, indeed, it is going through another phase of its major comeback, proving it never go out of style. First becoming a sign of glamour through Hollywood icons like Grace Kelly and Audrey Hepburn in the 1950s and 1960s. The bandana has evolve across different eras. But the fashion industry's renewed retro way once again brought it into the limelight. Indeed, the bandana scarf has become one of the most versatile styling accessories of the season. Here are 7 stylish ways to style a bandana scarf this summer. Retro Wrap The traditional bandana tie is arguably one of the most recognizable ways to tie a bandana and is still one of the best loved by fashion lovers every summer. Tie the bandana into a triangle shape, then put it on by tying it under your chin or neck for an old school look. It looks great paired with linen dresses, chunky sunglasses, and loose co-ords. Around The Neck Wearing a bandana around the neck is one of those fashion tricks that will never go out of style and will work to transform even the most basic of outfits. Simply fold it into a thin strip and tie it in a loose knot in the front, on the side, or in the back for an elegant look. It will pair perfectly well with everything from a classic white T-shirt to an off the shoulder tank top or a neat buttoned shirt. Scarf Headband Change up your usual hairstyle by creating a beautiful hairband out of your bandana. Fold it to make a long strip, put it on your head, and you’ll keep all loose hairs off your face while adding a pop of colour to your look. It goes perfectly well with beach waves, ponytails, messy buns, and braids. Hair Flair For those who love to add some understated style, wearing a bandana with a ponytail or bun can be the simplest method. Just tie it up on the band holding your hair in place, letting its edges fall freely for a pretty effect. The simple styling hack immediately elevates your otherwise plain hairstyles with added elements of motion and texture. As a Top A larger bandana scarf can also be used as a stylish top, especially during vacation and festival times. Depending on how you want to wear it, fold and knot it in a halter top or tube fashion or a backless one. You can style it with high waist jeans, denim shorts, linen pants, or maxi skirt, and add your favourite piece of accessories to complete the look. Bag Twist Revamp your favourite handbag for the season by wrapping a bandanna around its handle or making a bow out of it. This trick gives your handbag more colour and personality in an instant without the need for you to completely revamp your entire outfit. Bandannas with designs look great on woven totes, handbags, and canvas bags. Statement Wrap The bandana is not just for your hair or around your neck it also looks amazing as a wrist or belt accessory. Wrap it around your wrist for an easy burst of colour or wear it around your waist by looping it through your belt holes for a fun accent. You can style your bandana using this trick with jeans, tailored shorts, or flowing dresses. Also Read: Who Knew? These 90s Trends Are Making a Major Comeback

article_title: Monsoon Musings: For The Love Of Road Trips, Pasta, Soups, And WFH | Femina.in
sub_title: Managing Editor Primrose Monteiro DSouza shares what she loves about the monsoon, especially in the city that never sleeps.
article_content: Travel There are fewer visitors in the Sunshine State when the sun isn’t shining, but there is something undefinable that heals your soul as you sit and watch the rain drip – picturesquely – outside your window. And, after that rejuvenation, the dreaded trip back home is made more than bearable by the romance of the numerous waterfalls that cascade down the cliffs bordering the highway. Food It’s warming, filling, satisfying – you get a free pass when it comes to pasta in the rain. The monsoon is made for working on new pasta dishes. Faves have included making gnocchi and ravioli by hand, and watching out for new viral variations such as the feta-and-cherry-tomato pasta. Food Trying out new-to-me indulgent soup recipes is another rainy-day pleasure. And even your strictest nutritionist probably approves of all the Insta trends that show you how to make the creamiest variations without cream. The mushroom cappuccino – good enough to be on a restaurant menu – is a personal favourite from last year. Self Indulgence The monsoon can sound the death knell for any diet, but in such a delicious way. Burrowing under a blanket – alone or with SO, child, or bestie – is an essential rite of passage each year. And the snacks can be as indulgent as you like – crumbs be damned! Productivity If you miss the hybrid system, the rain might just be your ally. As the city floods and commuting becomes impossible, you get to stay home, be productive, and catch all the drama outside your window while you stay warm and dry inside. The monsoon is a season of many moods – cosy evenings, comfort films, steaming plates of pakoras, and spontaneous walks in the rain. The first raindrops hit the ground, petrichor fills the air, and, suddenly, everything feels a little greener, a lot slower, yet somehow more alive. Whether it’s curling up under a blanket with a good book, or gathering family for a game night when the rain keeps everyone indoors, the monsoon has a wonderful way of turning the most ordinary moments into unforgettable memories. article_content: Substance is not defined by success alone. It is shaped by the choices that build character, the courage to keep going when the path is difficult, and the impact one creates beyond personal milestones. Femina ’s Women Of Substance edition celebrates women who have led with conviction across business, cinema, sport, public life, education, art, design, and social change. Some have inherited powerful legacies and expanded them with purpose. Some have built institutions from the ground up. Some have turned personal challenges into platforms for change. Together, they remind us that true influence is not only about visibility; it is about responsibility, resilience, and the ability to inspire others. Manasi Kirloskar Tata; Aparna Piramal Raje; Rekha Across these pages are women who represent substance in its many compelling forms. Sushmita Sen continues to stand for individuality, freedom and self-belief, from becoming India’s first Miss Universe to defining motherhood and stardom on her own terms. Rekha remains one of Indian cinema’s most enigmatic icons, a performer who turned reinvention into an art form and dignity into a language of its own. Shubha Mudgal represents the power of artistic rigour, showing how classical tradition can remain deeply alive when approached with curiosity, discipline, and courage. In the world of business and enterprise, Falguni Nayar changed India’s beauty landscape by building Nykaa after a successful career in investment banking, proving that ambition does not come with an age limit. Suchita Oswal Jain has strengthened Vardhman Textiles with innovation, inclusion, and a future-facing leadership style rooted in legacy. Brahmani Nara brings a new lens to Heritage Foods, focusing on value-added growth, nutrition, farmer empowerment, and responsible business. Gita Gopinath , one of the world’s most influential economists, has shaped global thinking at the IMF and Harvard with clarity, scholarship, and authority. PV Sindhu; Natasha Poonawalla; Princess Mrinalika Bhanjdeo There are also women whose work has changed lives at the grassroots. Sunita Kohli has restored some of India’s most significant public interiors, including Rashtrapati Bhavan and the Prime Minister’s Office, reminding us that design can also be an act of cultural preservation. Safeena Husain , founder of Educate Girls, has spent years bringing out-of-school girls back into classrooms and making education a tool of dignity and agency. Rouble Nagi has used art, colour and community classrooms to transform underserved spaces into places of learning and hope. Bansuri Swaraj represents a new generation in public life, carrying legacy with awareness while building her own identity through law and service. The edition is anchored by cover star Dr Payal Kanodia , Chairperson and Trustee of M3M Foundation and Promoter of the M3M Group. A social entrepreneur, philanthropist, and athlete, she brings together seemingly different worlds with remarkable ease. Her work through the M3M Foundation spans health, education, women’s empowerment and sustainable development across 22 states, reflecting a commitment to building systems of support where they are needed most. Her journey is not only about leadership, but about channelling privilege, discipline and vision into work that creates measurable impact. What makes Dr Payal’s story especially powerful is the range of her identity. She is a philanthropist working at scale, a leader connected to community transformation, and a gold medallist in kettlebell lifting who has represented India on the global stage. Her sporting journey reflects discipline, resilience, and the ability to push personal limits. Her social work reflects empathy, structure, and the belief that meaningful change must touch lives in tangible ways. In a world that often asks women to choose one identity, she shows the strength of embracing many. In a fast-changing India, these women reflect the many ways leadership is being redefined today. They are building companies, preserving heritage, expanding access to education, shaping culture, representing India globally, and opening doors for those who come after them. They carry forward legacies, create new ones and show that substance is not about being celebrated for a moment, but about making work that continues to matter. article_title: Monsoon Musings: Chai, Cinema, Books, And Nostalgia | Femina.in
sub_title: Digital Editor Shilpa Dubey capture the cosy rituals, rainy-day escapes, old songs and simple pleasures that make  the monsoon musings so magical.
article_content: Nostalgia The rain always changes the pace of things a little. You walk more carefully so you don’t slip, you actually listen when thunder rolls in instead of scrolling through the day, and chai takes an extra minute or 10 because you’re in no rush to finish it. I pull my chair to the balcony, put on an old Lata Mangeshkar or Kishore Kumar number – something my mother used to hum while she cooked – and I just sit there, letting the song play through without skipping ahead. Old Bollywood melodies and the monsoon are made for each other. Nostalgia Some weekends I run off to a quiet, offbeat stay near Mumbai, chasing rainy mist over hills or a lake instead of city puddles and annoying traffic. Other days I don’t leave at all. I just slow down the house. Soup on the stove, sometimes a chocolate mud pie, and a film where I already know how the story ends. A ’90s marathon, maybe. Faces I’ve grown up with, plots I could recite. There’s comfort in knowing exactly what’s coming. Creativity At home I pull out old photo albums, because nostalgia and rain have always been the same season to me. Every photograph in the rain looks like it’s asking harder to be remembered. I reorganise shelves, rearrange rooms that were fine as they were. This year I want to try something new too, making paper from scraps I’ve saved, watching pulp turn into something whole again. There’s something about the monsoon that makes me want to remake things rather than just consume them. Books And then there’s Kitab Khana at Fort in Mumbai on a wet afternoon. It’s the way the pages smell different when the air is thick like this, and how I can lose an hour just standing between shelves not even reading, but just being near stories. Or the walk to Ashok Vada Pav. Umbrella in one hand, a piping-hot vada pav in another and the downpour all around you – if this is not the Mumbai monsoon, then what is! My hair disagrees with all this slow romance, so oiling and braiding become their own small ritual too. And, somewhere in between all of it, I always find myself glancing up, half expecting a rainbow. From Muse To Mogul: Meet India's New Era Of Celebrity Entrepreneurship

article_title: Niu Lai: A Bad Animation Masterpiece Or Human Slop? | Femina.in
sub_title: A mother-son duo spent five years making the viral Chinese movie Niu Lai. It might have one of the worst animations, but people can't stop watching it to beat the AI
article_content: Some people are calling it a Human Slop. For some, it’s “At least it’s not AI,” while others are defending it by saying, “Stop calling this movie slop,” because it isn’t made with a sloppy prompt or low effort. The movie Niu Lai (2026) was solely made by the Chinese mother-son duo Sun Lifang and Xin Yumeng. It took them around five years to complete, using second-hand hardware bought online. The movie’s budget was only a few thousand yuan, and it is currently earning millions at the box office. When I saw it trending online, I wondered if, similar to all the quick-gratification videos of construction, cleaning, and rom-com dramas of AI fruits that those addicted to short-form content watches today, this was anything alike. Initially, I thought people would watch anything that was put in front of them. But no, people are watching and supporting it for the realism it shows. I went in without too much context, especially about the genre. Without getting into spoilers, because it is worth watching, let me describe it for you. Niu Lai is like a fever dream. Some people on the internet even claim that it has effects similar to time dilation. Perhaps that is because of its dated format and setting, reminiscent of the old boxy computers we were used to seeing in the 90s. The movie begins with an unsettling peace in the forest/desert before taking us through the story of a baby cow/ox. Along the way, it explores childhood imagination, the importance of taking children’s questions seriously and the patience required to understand them. It also explores bonds such as those between mothers and children that hold families and communities together, while touching on fear, danger, migration and the things we do to overcome them. The movie also shows the destruction and deforestation caused by humans and their inventions along with what we are willing to sacrifice for something bigger than ourselves, and what family, friendship, kindness and courage really mean. Niu Lai asks questions such as: Why do we have to move or migrate? Why can’t I do it tomorrow, when I’ll be older than I am today? And somehow, despite all these underlying heavy questions, plot twists and subtleties, it is still fun, wholesome and, at times, comical. article_title: Inside Femina Circle Season 2: Amruta Khanvilkar on Sisterhood, Saris and Staying Rooted | Femina.in
sub_title: Amruta Khanvilkar celebrates sisterhood and sarees at Femina Circle, Pune — from career milestones to a masterclass in the art of draping.
article_content: Femina Circle Season 2 returned for its second session with an evening that felt less like an event and more like a homecoming. Held at Narrative, Pune, the gathering brought together women from all walks of life to celebrate community, connection, and the quiet power of women championing women. The star of the evening, actor and entrepreneur Amruta Khanvilkar, took the stage in a room full of familiar warmth. A proud daughter of Pune, Amruta’s journey has spanned Marathi and Hindi cinema alike – from her 2006 debut in Golmaal to the era-defining Wajle Ke Bara, a film that, 15 years on, remains a cultural touchstone for millennials and Gen Z. Her reality television innings on Nach Baliye and Khatron Ke Khiladi, alongside acclaimed film work in Raazi and Satyameva Jayate, has cemented her as one of Indian entertainment’s most versatile faces. More recently, she has stepped confidently into entrepreneurship with Amulya by Amruta, her own sari label that recently claimed an Emerging Luxury Sari Brand award. During the session, Amruta shared that saris have always been part of her life journey. In fact, her first job as a model was for a sari brand – she was paid Rs 500 to clotheshorse saris standing for over 24 hours! When her elder sister got married, she discovered that authentic Paithani saris weren’t easy to come by, and that inspired her to get authentic handloom saris made for her family. No conversation on saris would be complete without the art of draping them, and Pune-based draping artist Tejas Gursale brought exactly that – walking the audience through the artistry behind the perfect drape, drawing on his experience dressing brides and celebrities, including Amruta herself, for a session that was as instructive as it was elegant. Tejas showcased three very modern drape styles – styling the sari with a blazer, a corset, and a chiffon sari to make it look like a gown. The floor was then thrown open to the audience, with questions flowing freely before the evening closed with heartfelt thanks to both Amruta and Tejas, and a group photograph to mark the occasion.

article_title: When A Fandom Starts Feeling Like Home | Femina.in
sub_title: Sometimes, all it takes to feel a little less alone is finding a fandom where someone else is cheering for exactly the same thing.
article_content: It usually starts with something small. Maybe it’s a song you can’t stop replaying, a book you can’t put down, a TV show that makes you think about the characters as the credits roll, or a sports team that somehow affects your mood every weekend. Before you know it, you’re searching for theories on subreddits, sending memes on Instagram, joining conversations on X, or exchanging excited messages with strangers who understand how you feel. Finding Your People After spending years being online and immersed in fandoms, I know the thrill of waiting until midnight alongside millions of people worldwide. The countdown ends, a music video or new episode drops, and fans start dissecting lyrics, spotting Easter eggs, and sharing reactions in real time. A fan in Japan posts a translation within minutes, someone in Brazil explains a cultural reference, and another in London uploads fan edits. For those few hours, geography doesn't matter because you’re part of a community experiencing the same moment together. That feeling is everywhere. Just ask anyone who stayed up for the release of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows or raced through The Hunger Games to join the conversation and share their thoughts online. It’s the same feeling when thousands of Swifties sing the bridge to Taylor Swift’s Cruel Summer in unison, share friendship bracelets with strangers, or when fans fervently defend Team Jeremiah or Team Conrad after watching The Summer I Turned Pretty . In a fandom, media stops being something we consume alone and becomes something we all experience together, complete with the highs and, yes, even the lows. The K-Pop Effect K-pop fandoms might understand this best. Whether it’s ARMYs counting down to a BTS comeback, MOAs decoding TXT’s lore, or BLINKs celebrating BLACKPINK’s latest release, fans translate livestreams for international audiences, organise birthday fundraisers, swap photocards across continents, and line up overnight for concerts. Often, they leave with friendships and memories that might last longer than the groups they love. More Than Just A Game Few experiences compare to watching an entire stadium erupt after a last-minute goal or seeing millions celebrate a FIFA World Cup or Formula 1 victory together. Whether you’re refreshing the score every few seconds or celebrating with strangers at a watch party, fandoms make victories feel shared, and losses feel personal. These are people we might never meet, fictional worlds that don’t exist, and games whose outcomes we can’t control. Yet they become some of the most important parts of our lives. The Feeling of Belonging Psychologists often say that belonging is one of our most basic needs, and fandoms provide just that. Of course, some downsides exist, such as disagreements that turn toxic and unnecessary competition. But, for every fan war, there are countless quieter acts of kindness. Fans raise money for charity in an artist’s name, organise book swaps, create accessibility guides, hand out freebies at concerts, or simply check in on someone they’ve connected with over their favourite artist. When life feels overwhelming, fandoms can offer comfort and something to look forward to. Sometimes, the most crucial reminder we need is that, even when the world feels disconnected, there’s always someone else refreshing the same countdown, singing the same lyrics, or cheering for the same thing you are too. article_title: These UP Women Entrepreneurs Are Bringing Millets To Indian Kitchens | Femina.in
sub_title: These UP Women Entrepreneurs Are Bringing Millets To Indian Kitchens These UP Women Entrepreneurs Are Bringing Millets To Indian Kitchens
article_content: In Chandpur village in Uttar Pradesh’s Gonda district, a small group of women has empowered itself using traditional grains that have created modern opportunities. What began as a small effort to achieve financial independence has grown into a thriving millet business with an annual turnover of over ₹50 lakh. It is led by Neha Tiwari and Jyoti Mishra who, in turn, have inspired this 12-member self-help group, transforming locally-grown coarse grains into packaged products that are now sold both offline and online. These women from Parsapur town, dreamed of building a livelihood through their own efforts. They are supported by the National Rural Livelihood Mission that has helped them turn their vision into reality. When the idea first came about, very few believed that the millet products they produce – marketed under the brand name ‘ Nityam Bhog ’ – would become an online brand. But, within just three years since its inception, their small self-help group has already achieved an annual turnover of over Rs 50 lakh. This remarkable journey is now inspiring many others. Small Beginnings Today, many women across Uttar Pradesh have become symbols of empowerment for building successful livelihoods through self-help groups. Neha Tiwari from Chandpur joined the National Rural Livelihood Mission in 2023 and went on to establish the Nityam Mahila Swayam Sahayata Samuh. It is aptly named, ‘Nityam’ – which means ‘daily’ – reflecting their effort that is built through consistent effort every single day. According to Neha, “We believe that self-reliance is not achieved in a single day; it is built through daily hard work and continuous effort. With this belief, we named the group ‘Nityam Mahila Swayam Sahayata Samuh.’” The group initially began with 12 women. Their resources were limited, but their determination was immense. The first challenge that they faced was arranging capital funds. Easy access to self-employment loans under the National Rural Livelihood Mission made it easier, and the group ventured into millet production. They began cleaning, milling, and packaging traditional coarse grains such as maize, barley, bajra, ragi , gram, sawa, kodo, kakun , and jowar all by themselves. Soon, multigrain flour and different millet flours in packs under the ‘ Nityam Bhog ’ brand started reaching areas such as Gonda, Balrampur, Bahraich, Ayodhya, and Lucknow. Packaged in 500 g, 1 kg and 2 kg sizes, the millet products quickly found their way to kitchens beyond their village. Jyoti Mishra, who leads the group alongside Neha, says that demand for millet products increases several times during the winter season. Due to growing awareness about nutrition and about the health benefits of coarse grains, urban consumers are increasingly reaching out for these products. The group’s annual turnover has now reached between Rs 50 lakh and Rs 60 lakh, and the profits are distributed equally among all members. This has brought a significant improvement in the economic condition of these women. Many have started operating bank accounts in their own names for the first time. Their children’s education has improved, and they no longer have to depend on others to meet their household needs. Their confidence has also increased. Women who once hesitated to step outside their homes now discuss business, manage orders, and negotiate in the market. Jyoti says that the journey of expanding their product range is continuing. In the days to come, the group plans to introduce products such as papad , pickles, and incense sticks. The Making Of Success Success does not come overnight. It is driven by hard work and dedication, but government policies play a significant role as well. When the government led by Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath transformed the National Rural Livelihood Mission from a government scheme into a medium of social transformation, people began to see new pathways in life. Easy loans, business training, market linkages, and access to digital platforms have helped transform rural women from being beneficiaries into entrepreneurs. Today, Nityam Bhog products are available on Amazon through the Arga brand, marking an important milestone in the group’s journey. What began as a village-based enterprise is now reaching customers far beyond its local community. Within just three years, this enterprise has crossed an annual turnover of more than Rs 50 lakh, serving as living proof that rural women can set global benchmarks of success if they receive the right opportunities and resources. The group has now become a source of inspiration for other women in Chandpur village. Young women and girls from the village regularly approach Neha and Jyoti to learn how to start a business. Priyanka Niranjan, the District Magistrate of Gonda, says, “This transformation reflects the self-reliance of women. The government has resolved to make women self-reliant by connecting them with government schemes. For this, we are continuously forming self-help groups under the National Rural Livelihood Mission. The efforts of the Nityam group are commendable and will boost the confidence of other women.” “I had wanted to do something on my own for a long time, but I couldn't find the right path,” Neha confides. “When I joined the National Rural Livelihood Mission, it felt as though the government was holding my hand. Today, seeing our Nityam Bhog products being sold on Amazon fills me with a happiness and pride that words cannot express.” Also Read: #WomenForWomen: Indian Women Entrepreneurs

article_title: UP State: Striving For A Fair & Better Future For The Country’s Youth | Femina.in
sub_title: Under the tenure of Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, Uttar Pradesh enacted one of the country's toughest anti-cheating laws for a better future.
article_content: The Uttar Pradesh government continues to work to curb unfair examination and recruitment practices through stricter laws and stronger administration. By Brij Lal, Rajya Sabha MP and Former Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh In Uttar Pradesh, a vast majority of the youth see competitive examinations as the pathway to their future. When merit does not receive a fair opportunity, it inevitably leads to frustration and disillusionment. The future of the state's youth depends on the integrity of examination halls and the fairness of recruitment boards. Over the past few years, under the tenure of Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, the state enacted one of the country's toughest anti-cheating laws to dismantle cheating syndicates. Undoing Unfairness The character of any government is reflected in its decisions. Over the years, under the governance of previous parties, Uttar Pradesh saw its fair share of problems. The policy of allowing students to take examinations at their own schools, commonly known as the ‘self-centre’ system was retained. Although it appeared to be a routine administrative decision, its long-term consequences proved deeply damaging. Under the cover of this policy, a parallel network gradually emerged across the state, which later came to be known as the cheating mafia. The impact of the then government’s leniency soon became evident in examination results. In 2004, the Intermediate examination pass percentage rose dramatically, a trend that appeared less a reflection of genuine academic improvement than of systemic laxity. The greatest tragedy was that students who had worked hard and relied solely on merit found themselves pushed aside, while organised cheating networks continued to profit. This weakening of educational standards continued to harm the state's academic environment for years. With the change of power between 2012 and 2017, the people expected the introduction of meaningful reforms in recruitment processes. However, the situation reportedly deteriorated with the credibility of competitive examinations suffering repeated setbacks. Hardly any major recruitment board escaped allegations of irregularities or question paper leaks. The leakage of the medical entrance examination paper from the treasury shattered the dreams of lakhs of aspirants and ultimately forced the examination to be cancelled. Similarly, the question paper for one of the state's most prestigious civil services examinations was leaked through social media, leaving the authorities with no option but to cancel the examination following widespread protests. The recruitment process for the post of Village Development Officer also came under scrutiny after a sting operation exposed bribery, with allegations of involvement by influential individuals associated with the ruling party. During this period, cheating and question paper leaks increasingly came to be viewed as systemic features of the examination process. Another notable aspect of this period was that while recruitment in most government departments was conducted through the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission and the Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission, nepotism became a defining feature of recruitment. The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission, an institution regarded as the backbone of a fair democratic recruitment system, faced serious allegations. A public interest litigation was filed before the High Court questioning the disproportionately high selection of candidates belonging to a particular caste group and presenting data alleging significant imbalance in the selection process. Such allegations fuelled widespread resentment among meritorious candidates from other communities, many of whom felt that caste and political proximity had become more influential than merit in determining selection. Similar controversies also surrounded police recruitment. After evidence reportedly emerged of large-scale irregularities, political recommendations and bribery in the recruitment of thousands of constables and Provincial Armed Constabulary personnel, the government constituted an inquiry committee, whose report pointed to serious irregularities. The matter remained tied up in courts for years, illustrating the depth of the alleged problems within the recruitment system. Heralding A New Era After 2017, the approach of the Yogi Adityanath government marked a clear policy shift. The government treated the disorder within the examination system as a serious administrative challenge and chose to address it through legislative intervention. This led to the enactment of the Uttar Pradesh Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, widely known as the anti-cheating law. The legislation is regarded as one of the strictest in the country, prescribing penalties of up to life imprisonment and fines of up to ₹1 crore for those involved in question paper leaks or organised cheating. It also provides for the attachment of the assets of examination agencies found guilty and enables the government to recover the entire cost of conducting the examination from them. Alongside these legal measures, several administrative reforms were also implemented. Greater care was exercised in selecting examination centres, CCTV surveillance was made mandatory, multi-layered security arrangements were introduced for safeguarding question papers, and administrative accountability on examination days was strengthened. As a result, a state where question paper leaks had once become almost synonymous with major competitive examinations began conducting large-scale examinations in a comparatively smooth and orderly manner. The lives of millions of young aspirants depend on the outcome of a single examination. It goes without saying that a fair examination and recruitment system alone can ensure that merit receives its rightful recognition. article_title: The Bare Bar: Elevating Everyday Personal Care | Femina.in
sub_title: In conversation with The Bare Bar's Founder, Radhika Mukhija, and Co-Founder, Dhruv Mukhija on how they’re shaping their brand's next chapter.
article_content: Starting as a hands-on pursuit of formulation and product-making and evolving into a homegrown body-care brand, The Bare Bar has come a long way. The brand was founded in 2020 by Radhika Mukhija, with the belief that everyday personal care could be made more thoughtfully. Cut to the present, she still leads product development, formulation and manufacturing, and remains closely involved in everything from ingredient selection to the final scent of a product. Her son, Dhruv Mukhija, joined in as Co-Founder in 2024, bringing experience in brand building, marketing, and growth. He now leads The Bare Bar’s brand strategy, sales, partnerships and expansion, while Radhika continues to anchor the product and manufacturing side of the company. Together, the mother-son dup are shaping The Bare Bar’s next chapter. Excerpts from an interview… You built The Bare Bar by formulating every product yourself in-house. What was one formulation lesson you learned then that guides how you develop products today? Radhika Mukhija: One of the biggest lessons I learnt early on was that a formulation can look perfect on paper and still not work perfectly for the person using it. You can have the right ingredients, the right percentages and something that feels beautiful in the lab, but what really matters is how it performs in someone’s everyday life. That has stayed with me. Today, I think about the entire experience of a product how it feels, how it performs in our climate, how it fits into a routine and whether someone will genuinely want to use it again. Formulation is not just about putting good ingredients together; it is about solving a real problem well. What’s something from those early days that you still do today in the lab? RM: I still test and retest products far more than I probably need to. In the early days, because I was doing everything myself, I became very hands-on with every stage of the process. I would make something, use it myself, observe how it changed over time and then go back to the formulation. That habit has stayed. I still believe that you cannot develop products only by looking at a formulation sheet. You have to experience the product yourself and understand what it is actually doing. Indian weather, hard water, humidity all of that impacts how body care products perform. What’s a challenge specific to India and how are you working on it? RM: India is not one climate, and that makes body care particularly interesting. We have humidity, heat, dry weather, hard water, and very different lifestyles across the country. A product that works beautifully in one environment may behave very differently somewhere else. We are increasingly developing with these realities in mind rather than treating them as an afterthought. We look at things like how a product feels on skin in humidity, how quickly it absorbs, how it performs through a long day and how it fits into an Indian routine. For us, performance has to be tested against real life, not just a controlled environment. You made a deliberate shift from “ingredient-led clean beauty” to “performance-first body care for Indian conditions.” What was the moment or customer feedback that made you realise that shift was necessary? RM: It came from listening to customers. We started noticing that people weren’t necessarily asking us for more ingredients or more complicated formulations. They were asking very practical questions: “Will this actually work in our weather? Will it last through the day? Will it feel comfortable? Will it work with my routine?” That made us realise that being “clean” or natural could not be the end point. People want products that align with their values, but they also expect them to perform. That was an important shift for us from talking primarily about what goes into a product to asking what the product actually does for the person using it. What are some non-negotiables you refuse to compromise on with your products and in your personal life? RM: With products, I won’t compromise on performance, safety or honesty. If something doesn’t work the way it should, I don’t think we should put it out simply because it looks good on paper or because it is commercially convenient. Personally, I value curiosity and staying close to the work. Building a brand can very quickly become about meetings, numbers and deadlines, but I don’t want to become disconnected from the actual products and the people using them. I think staying curious and being willing to question what you’re doing is something I want to hold on to. You joined the brand to lead sales and growth while Radhika anchors product. Where do your visions most often clash and where do they align perfectly? Dhruv Mukhija: I wouldn’t say our visions clash as much as the way we arrive at decisions does. There is obviously a generational difference in how we work. My mother has years of experience and is a lot more instinctive, whereas I naturally look at things through sales data, financials, market opportunity, and what we can realistically scale. Where we probably debate the most is the portfolio. She is a creator at heart, so when she makes something she really believes in, she wants to put it out into the market. My role is usually to ask whether we have a right to win in that category, whether the market is large enough and whether it really fits what The Bare Bar should stand for. Where we are completely aligned is on what we are trying to build. We want to create clean, high-performance body care for India that feels aspirational but is still accessible. How we get there, how quickly we get there, and how many products we need along the way is where most of the back and forth happens. In body care, people switch products often. What’s one product or product experience you’re offering to make someone stay with The Bare Bar? DM: Our new deodorants are probably the best example of what we are trying to do as a brand. Clean deodorants that genuinely perform have been difficult to find in India, and our three-ingredient odour-neutralising system gives up to 24-hour odour control. In India, where heat, humidity and sweat are such a big part of everyday life, that performance really matters. But I also think the reason someone stays with The Bare Bar has to go beyond one product. We put a lot of thought into the scent and sensorial experience across the range. Our Warm Vanilla Body Wash has real vanilla pods in it, our Rose & Oats Body Wash has oats for gentle exfoliation, and we use details like lavender buds in other products. For us, the product has to work first. But if it also smells great, feels great, and gives you an experience you actually look forward to using, that is what makes people come back. How do you make decisions when “product instinct” and “consumer data” disagree? Can you give us an example? DM: At this stage of the business, consumer data is extremely important to us. Once you have been in the market for some time, there is a lot you can learn from what people are actually buying, repeating, responding to and dropping off from. Because we manufacture in-house, we can take those learnings back into product development. It could be something around packaging, functionality, scent, format or even how people are using the product. Where instinct becomes more important is when we are trying something that does not really exist in the market yet. In that case, there may not be historical data to rely on. So we combine our product instinct with qualitative consumer feedback and try to understand whether the problem we are solving is actually meaningful. Scent is a good example because it is so subjective. You need instinct to create something distinctive, but you also need consumers to tell you whether it resonates. Once the product is in the market, though, the data becomes much harder to argue with. What’s one misconception Indian consumers have about “clean” or “natural” body care that you’re trying to unlearn for them? DM: I think one misconception is that natural automatically means better. A product can be 100% natural and still not necessarily be the most effective formulation or the best choice for every person. Even natural ingredients have to be used thoughtfully and at the right levels. The other misconception is that clean body care either has to be expensive or that you buy it mainly because it feels like a better choice, rather than because it performs. That is the gap we are trying to bridge. We want to show that you can have products with a very high proportion of naturally derived ingredients, formulate them thoughtfully, and still deliver really strong performance at a price point that is aspirational but accessible. For me, clean should never be the reason you compromise on how well the product works. Three years from now, what would make you say “we did it” , is it a product metric, a trust metric, or something else? DM: For me, it would ultimately come down to repeat and customer love. Of course revenue and scale matter – we are building a business, but the strongest proof for me would be seeing people repeatedly come back to The Bare Bar because they genuinely want the product again, not because we pushed another ad or offered another discount. I would love to reach a point where someone sees The Bare Bar online or on a shelf and already knows what to expect from us. There is trust in the product, trust in the brand, and a willingness to try whatever we launch next because we have earned that credibility. Three years from now, I want The Bare Bar to sit at the intersection of clean, high-performance body care that is made for India, in India, by Indians. If we have strong repeat behaviour and people genuinely feel an affinity towards the brand, that is when I would feel we have really built something. article_title: Megha And Pritesh Asher On Building Juicy Chemistry Without Compromising On What Matters | Femina.in
sub_title: Megha and Pritesh Asher take us inside Juicy Chemistry’s journey from a ₹5,000 kitchen experiment to an internationally recognised brand.
article_content: In 2014, Juicy Chemistry began in a 10-by-10 kitchen in Coimbatore with a blender, ₹5,000, and a simple idea that skincare should be honest about what goes into it. Founded by Megha and Pritesh Asher, the brand started with handmade soaps and cold-pressed oils, and what began with friends and family as its first customers has grown into a brand built around transparency, conscious sourcing, and a refusal to compromise on its standards. For Megha, the journey was also deeply personal. Years of dealing with PCOD, acne-prone, and sensitive skin led her to question the ingredients and promises behind conventional skincare. For Pritesh, his background in petrochemicals made him question products marketed as natural and organic when their ingredient lists told a different story. Together, those questions and experiences became the foundation of Juicy Chemistry. Femina: Juicy Chemistry started with Rs 5,000 and a 10-by-10 kitchen in Coimbatore. What inspired you to start the brand? Megha Asher: Honestly, it was not inspiration. It was frustration. Pritesh came from a petrochemicals background. One day, he picked up a product in a mall, labelled natural and organic, and turned the bottle around. He recognised the ingredients. The same compounds he had worked with in manufacturing. We put it back on the shelf and went home. I had been dealing with PCOD for years. Sensitive, reactive skin and a beauty industry that kept selling me things that promised to fix it. I had tried enough products to understand that most of them were not telling the whole truth. So we asked a simple question. What if we made something that actually matched its claims? We started in our kitchen with cold-pressed oils and handmade soaps. Our first circle of friends and family became our first testers, our first honest critics, and eventually our first loyal customers. Their feedback shaped everything. The first time someone came back and said this actually worked, something shifted in us. We knew this was not just a kitchen experiment anymore. Transparency has always been central to Juicy Chemistry. How do you maintain that while working in an industry driven by beauty trends and aspiration? Megha: By deciding early that we would rather grow slowly on our terms than quickly on someone else's. The COSMOS V4 certification from Ecocert France is what makes transparency structural for us rather than just a value we claim. It is not self-declared. An independent body audits our ingredients, our supply chain, our processing, and our packaging. We cannot call something organic unless that claim has been externally verified. That removes the temptation to follow a trend that would compromise the standard because the certification makes compromise impossible. We have sat out trends that did not align with our formulation principles. We have said no to things that would have grown the brand faster but muddied what it stands for. Every one of those decisions felt uncomfortable in the moment. None of them feel uncomfortable in retrospect. The harder version of transparency is being honest about what a product can and cannot do. Skincare can support healthy skin. It cannot perform miracles. We try to stay on the right side of that line even when the industry norm is to exaggerate. Our customers notice. It is one of the reasons they come back. A post shared by Juicy Chemistry (@juicy_chemistry) What do you hope consumers understand about the difference between organic skincare and effective skincare through Juicy Actives? Megha: That it is a false choice and always has been. For a long time, consumers were told they had to pick. Effective or clean. Science-led actives on one side, organic formulations on the other. The assumption baked into that choice was that certification and performance were incompatible. We never believed that. Juicy Actives is the proof. Biocompatible actives combined with a certified organic formulation. The same COSMOS standard that governs our entire range, applied to a performance skincare line. Real, measurable results without compromising what goes onto your skin. What I hope consumers take from it is permission. Permission to want both. You do not have to choose between a product that works and a product you can trust. That has been Juicy Chemistry's argument since the beginning. Juicy Actives makes it undeniable. More than 60% of your customers are returning customers. What do you think keeps them coming back? Megha: The products work. That is the most honest answer I have. We have never had viral moments or big celebrity campaigns driving spikes in first-time buyers. What we have is a customer who tried something, noticed a real difference, and came back. There is also something deeper about trust. When a customer reads our label and finds that what is inside matches exactly what we said was inside, they experience something increasingly rare in this market. They feel they have not been misled. That feeling is quiet but it is powerful. It compounds over time and it becomes loyalty that no discount or trend can undo. We also have customers who have been with us since the very beginning. They write to us. They tell us what their skin needs next. They notice when something changes. That relationship, where the customer is genuinely part of how the brand grows, is something no marketing budget can buy or replicate. Both founders come from very different professional backgrounds. How have those differences shaped the way you run Juicy Chemistry? Megha: Entirely, and mostly for the better. Pritesh sees every decision through the lens of formulation integrity. His question is always whether the ingredient is genuinely what it claims to be, whether the process is right, and whether it meets the standard. He has an instinct for the gap between what something says it is and what it actually is. That instinct is the founding principle of this brand. My background is in criminology and journalism. Those sound completely unrelated to skincare. They are not. Criminology taught me to look at systems, to understand how harm gets normalised, and to ask who benefits when things stay the way they are. Journalism taught me to communicate precisely and to be accountable to evidence. Together, they gave me a way of looking at the beauty industry that goes beyond products and trends. Where we create friction, it is useful friction. Pritesh will not compromise on the formulation, ever. I will push for communication that brings more people into the conversation. The negotiation between those two positions has produced something that holds its standard and still finds a way to grow. I would not change the dynamic for anything. As you expand internationally, what values do you want to keep unchanged? Megha: The certification standard and the honesty about what our products can do. The COSMOS V4 certification is internationally legible in a way that no Indian self-regulatory standard is. In the UAE, in Australia, and in France, consumers and retailers understand what COSMOS means the moment they see it. We will not lower that standard to make distribution easier, even when the pressure exists to do so. The certification is not a marketing asset we carry into new markets. It is the operating standard we refuse to leave behind. The other thing I am determined to protect is our directness. We do not oversell. We do not promise what our products cannot deliver. In markets even more saturated with beauty exaggeration than India, that restraint will either confuse people or attract exactly the consumer we want. We are comfortable with that uncertainty because we know which consumer we are building for. And underneath all of it, the pride in where we come from. We are an Indian brand that built something to a global standard, from the ground up, on our own terms. That identity does not change as we grow. If anything, it becomes more important to hold on as the brand reaches further. Looking back at the last 12 years, how would you describe the journey? Megha: Twelve years of firsts, honestly. We were among the first Indian skincare brands to pursue COSMOS V4 certification from Ecocert France, the most rigorous certified organic standard available globally. Getting there meant rebuilding our entire supply chain from scratch. Every ingredient had to be traceable to the soil it was grown in. The soil itself has to be conditioned for three years before it can bear fully organic produce. It took two years and complete honesty about what we had been doing wrong. When we achieved certification in 2017, we became one of the very few Indian brands to hold this standard. That was a first. When we launched the Bare With Us campaign, built on real, unretouched skin at a moment when AI filters were becoming the industry norm, that was a first. When we launched Juicy Actives, India's first certified organic performance skincare range, bringing biocompatible actives into the certified organic category, that was a first. Each of these firsts cost us something in the short term. None of them was the fastest or most commercially convenient path. But they built something that is very hard to replicate: a brand that has held its standard for twelve years without compromising it once. The Rs 5,000 kitchen standard and the 2026 standard are the same standard. That continuity is what I am most proud of. Where do you see Juicy Chemistry five years from now? Megha: A proudly made in India brand, recognised globally for what Indian organic formulation is truly capable of. We started small, and we now ship to over 30 countries. The COSMOS V4 certification we hold is internationally recognized in the UAE, Australia, and France, in ways that no Indian self-regulatory standard is. When a retailer or consumer in those markets sees our certification, they do not need us to explain it. That is a remarkable position for an Indian brand to be in, and we intend to build on it. On the product side, Juicy Actives is the most significant thing we have launched since the brand itself. The next five years will demonstrate that Indian certified organic formulation can sit alongside the best performance skincare in the world. Not as a compromise. As a choice people actively make because the results speak for themselves. Most importantly, I want the standard we have held for twelve years to become a standard the Indian beauty industry moves toward. We are not interested in being the only brand doing this properly. We are interested in raising what consumers expect. Five years from now, if more people in India and globally are reading labels, asking what certified organic actually means, and choosing products that can answer that question, Juicy Chemistry will have done something meaningful. That is the ambition. Rooted in India. Recognised everywhere. Also Read: Jui Talks About Building Her Brand From The Ground Up

article_title: Entrepreneur Tapur Gupta Is Making Skincare Simpler With Root Labs | Femina.in
sub_title: With skincare brand Root Labs, founder Tapur Gupta is challenging the more-is-more approach with minimal, barrier-first formulas for Indian skin.
article_content: At just 24, beauty entrepreneur Tapur Gupta is shaping what skincare needs to look like in India. As the founder of Root Labs, she is building a hormone-considerate, barrier-first skincare brand around a deceptively simple idea: skin does not need fixing; it needs support. “I believe our skin already knows how to heal itself. It doesn’t need to be constantly corrected or overwhelmed with stronger actives and complicated routines,” she says. Tapur’s own skincare journey sparked the shift. After an elaborate, active-heavy routine began working against her skin in India’s humid and pollution-heavy environment, she stripped it back and watched her barrier recover. That experience became the foundation for Root Labs, her brand that combines her psychology background, industry experience, and consumer-first approach to create uncomplicated skincare products. Every Root Labs formulation is built around hormone-safe ingredients and engineered specifically for Indian skin and climate, accounting for higher melanin levels, humidity, pollution, and near-constant sun exposure, rather than importing formulas designed for other skin types and climates. Today, Tapur runs product development, formulation strategy, and brand direction end-to-end, working closely with in-house manufacturing and testing teams to keep every launch tied to real consumer feedback rather than trend cycles. You built an elaborate, ingredient-led routine in Singapore that actually worked – then it backfired the moment you moved back to India. Walk us through what that unravelling actually looked like on your skin. When I was in Singapore, I started my mornings with a gentle face wash, exfoliating toner, a hyaluronic acid serum, niacinamide, a new active of choice every two months, moisturiser, sunscreen, and a quick round of gua sha. At night, I used peptides and retinol. I layered multiple actives because, honestly, my skin was loving it. It was clear, smooth, and I felt like I was doing everything right. When I moved back to India, that same routine slowly began to work against me. My skin became much more sensitive, irritated easily, and, for the first time in my life, I started breaking out. I was caught off guard, and my first instinct was to fix it with even more skincare. I started using a AHA 30% + BHA 2% peel, a salicylic acid toner, face masks and other actives. In trying to fix my skin, I was actually making it worse and eventually broke my skin barrier. And then I just gave up on the elaborate routine. I’d always had good skin, even through school, so I went back to basics: a gentle cleanser, simple moisturiser and sunscreen. I gave my skin some time, and it slowly healed itself. Stripping down to a cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen sounds simple to describe, but it must have felt counterintuitive after years of “more actives, more steps.” What made you trust that instinct instead of reaching for something stronger? Honestly, it wasn’t that I knew a gentle routine would fix my skin. I just reached a point where I didn’t know what else to try. I had spent so much time adding actives and experimenting, and nothing was helping. I just reached a point where I didn’t know what else to try, so I gave up on the elaborate routine altogether. I just focused on the basics: a gentle cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen. There was no big skincare epiphany at the time. I was just tired of experimenting with my skin. Slowly, my skin started recovering. I gave my skin time, and it healed itself. I realised I didn’t need to keep interfering. Sometimes, your skin just needs the right support and the space to do its job. Root Labs’ whole premise is that skincare rarely accounts for how our needs shift across hormonal life stages – puberty, pregnancy, menopause. What’s a specific piece of consumer feedback that first alerted you to this gap? Before this, I had never really thought about skincare as something that should change with your life stage or hormonal cycle. I assumed it was mostly about your skin type and concerns. While we were sampling for Root Labs, I decided to make the most of my social circle. Around Bhai Dooj , I created kits for my maasis, maamis, buas , cousins, and friends across different ages and life stages. A week later, when I went back to collect the first round of feedback, I realised the hesitation to try new skincare products was much bigger than I had expected. One aunt was pregnant and wanted to consult her doctor before using anything. Someone with extremely sensitive skin was apprehensive about trying a new product. Another had a young daughter and was hesitant about what was appropriate for her. That’s when it really clicked for me: people weren’t asking, ‘Will this work for my skin?’ They were asking, ‘Is this right for me, at this stage of my life?’ And that was a gap I felt skincare wasn’t really addressing. You studied consumer psychology at NTU before working across Coco Veda, Coco & Eve, and Nykaa Fashion. How much of Root Labs’ voice do you think comes directly from that academic background versus what you observed on the industry side? It’s a combination of both. Studying consumer psychology taught me to understand what makes people connect with and trust a brand, while my industry experience showed me how easily skincare can seem too technical or intimidating. With Root Labs, I wanted everything to feel relatable, casual, and conversational, like you’re talking to a friend, rather than being spoken down to by a brand. ‘Hormone-safe’ and ‘hormone-considerate’ aren’t terms most Indian consumers are fluent in yet. How do you explain this positioning to someone walking into it cold, without it sounding clinical or intimidating? We start with things people already experience instead of explaining the complicated science behind it. Your skin can change throughout your menstrual cycle because your hormones fluctuate, and the same happens during puberty, pregnancy, postpartum, and menopause. We also know that our skin can absorb certain chemicals, so we believe it's important to be mindful of what we’re putting on it. For us, hormone-considerate skincare simply means being more thoughtful about the ingredients we use, and building a strong skin barrier that can keep up with these hormonal changes. We also believe education should be bite-sized, not overwhelming. We break down things like hormones, ingredients, and the skin barrier into simple, relatable pieces, so consumers understand what they're putting on their skin without feeling like they need a degree in skincare. You’ve said Root Labs formulates specifically for Indian skin and climate – higher melanin, humidity, pollution, sun exposure – rather than adapting global formulas. What does that actually change in a formulation, practically speaking? Practically, it means we don’t just take a formula that works elsewhere and assume it will work the same way in India. We think about melanin, humidity, pollution, sun exposure, hard water, and the sensitivity of Indian skin when developing our products. We also consider how practical a product is for everyday use. Some ingredients, like vitamin C, can be quite unstable and require careful storage and handling to maintain stability. Rather than expecting consumers to get all of that right, we’d rather choose ingredients and formulations that are more stable and forgiving. Poorly stored or degraded products can contribute to irritation or sensitivity. We’re also careful with harsh actives and over-exfoliation because irritation can trigger inflammation and pigmentation, particularly in melanin-rich skin. And a big part of this is feedback. Our brand ambassador community constantly tests our products across different skin types and conditions, and that feedback goes straight back into our R&D. So we’re continuously learning and refining rather than assuming one formula works for everyone. Nine months between starting development and launch is fast for a science-backed skincare brand. What did you have to get comfortable being imperfect about, and what did you refuse to compromise on? For Root Labs, product development doesn't end at launch. We knew from the beginning that we would be a brand that keeps evolving through feedback. Since we manufacture in-house, we can take customer feedback, go back to the lab, and actually refine our formulations and products. We were okay with being imperfect when it came to things like packaging. For example, we initially wanted to avoid monocartons to reduce packaging waste (explained here), but customer feedback made us realise they were important, so we changed our approach. What we refused to compromise on was the formulation. Every ingredient, percentage, texture and claim has to have a reason behind it. We'd rather launch fewer products and keep improving them than rush something just to add another SKU. You were 23 when you started building this and are 24 now, genuinely one of the youngest founders in Indian skincare. Has your age worked against you in rooms with manufacturers, investors or retailers, and how have you navigated that? With manufacturers and suppliers, being young definitely works against me sometimes. There are moments when they don’t take me seriously initially because I’m 24 and they I’m working on a ‘hobby’. But that usually changes once we start discussing the product. When I explain why we've chosen a particular ingredient, percentage, texture or formulation, and the thinking behind every decision, they realise I know my brand inside out. I don’t try to prove myself based on my age. I let the work and how deeply I understand the product speak for me. The brand talks about not fixing skin but supporting it: a fairly quiet, patient promise in a category that usually sells transformation and speed. Has that been a hard sell to a market conditioned to expect visible results fast? It’s only been seven months for us, so we’re still figuring out what works best. But we’ve been very transparent from the beginning about how our products work and what consumers should realistically expect from them. The transparency helps build trust. We’ve seen this especially at our pop-ups and events. When I personally explain a product, why we formulated it the way we did, and what it is actually meant to do, the response is always very positive. People ask questions, they understand the thought behind it, and we’ve had some of our best compliments and sales from those conversations. When people realise that I genuinely know what I’m making and why I’m making it, they trust the brand a little more. You mentioned building Root Labs nudged you away from being ‘a serious makeup person’ toward minimalism. Has founding this brand changed how you personally think about beauty, or just about skincare? Definitely. I used to be much more into makeup, but over time I've realised I really enjoy the feeling of almost bare skin. I like keeping things light, letting my skin breathe, and not feeling like I have too many layers on. Even on days when I have a breakout or feel like I need to cover it, I usually don’t want to aggravate it further with a heavy layer of makeup. I’d rather leave my skin alone and give it the time and space to heal on its own. And honestly, building Root Labs has only reinforced that for me. Being comfortable going bare-faced has also meant I get to actually show what Root Labs has done for my skin. Also Read: Syndiora’s Ankita Gupta Is Championing Lab-Grown Diamond Jewellery in India

article_content: Femina Circle Season 2 was kicked off in Pune with an evening centred around meaningful conversations, inspiring stories and new connections.
